reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it opens with a summary, explains in a separate section what the diagram leaves out, puts every failure mode in one table, and works through a Retry-After example, while A is tighter but cites requirement numbers ("req. 3") an outsider cannot look up.

author: sonnet
reason: A suits a newcomer better because it defines Redis, Lua scripts and fixed windows in plain terms and puts every failure case in one table that is easy to scan; B is somewhat more rigorous, with its worked 100th/101st example and late-answer overcount, but it leans on "req. N" references an outsider has never seen.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to pick up cold: it opens with a summary that gives the reasons and the current scale (rows, traffic, server names), has a table of where state lives, and splits the rollout into named phases with sub-steps, while A's terms list is longer and its mechanism descriptions are denser and harder to orient in.

author: haiku
reason: A is easier for an outsider to follow: its summary says why the plan is shaped this way, one flag with five named states shows every mode, a table says where each piece of state lives, and the phased checklist reads in order, while B is more precise in places but denser and spreads the same model across more sections and mechanisms.

author: sonnet
reason: B makes the moving parts easier to follow for a newcomer: one named copy function used by every path, a fence that decides routing instead of relying on flag-cache timing, a state table, and a closing failure-to-effect table, whereas A's design is equally careful but is harder to reason about because it leans on 30 s cache timing arithmetic and an overloaded max-INT version trick.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for an outsider to build a mental model from: it defines every moving part up front (fence, outbox, relay, copy function, tombstones, flags with defaults), gives one numbered write path, and ends with tables for where state lives and what each failure does, whereas B, though more detailed on edge cases such as GTID catch-up and the version column, spreads its mechanisms across prose and checklist steps.

author: haiku
reason: A is longer and denser, but it defines every moving part (freeze marker, due list, charge record, idempotency key) and gives each rollback step with the reason it is safe, so a newcomer can see how double charges and dropped charges are actually prevented; B's rollback steps are too terse and its charge-ownership claim is asserted, not explained.

author: haiku
reason: A gives a newcomer a clear model quickly: a short glossary, a clean nested-state diagram, the same Starts/Does/Gate layout for each mode, and five plain rollback steps. B is more exhaustive, but its many terms, edge-case rules and 14 open questions make the core mechanism harder to pick out on first reading.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the mechanics more precisely and consistently: how the freeze reaches the workers, how reconciliation checks the ledger against the payment provider, how workers that missed the flag change are stopped, and why the flag changes last. B's diagram and step list disagree on the number and order of the rollback steps, and B checks only the ledger when deciding what was already charged.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains how the parts actually work, where A only names them: the rollout controller, the checkpoints, how workers see the freeze, how the ledger is reconciled against the payment provider, and what happens when the config service is unreachable. A is shorter but leaves gaps an outsider would trip on, such as trusting the ledger alone for in-flight charges and the slip "steps 3 is skipped".

author: haiku
reason: A is the one I would rather be handed: its flowchart nodes carry the same step numbers as the text, and it spells out how the parts actually work (outbox relay, broker acknowledgement and redelivery, a webhook arriving before provider_ref is stored, how Cart learns each outcome), while B reads more easily but has a confusing diagram where refund outcomes come out of the charge-outcome node, and it wrongly says the stock has always been sold to someone else.

author: haiku
reason: I'd rather be handed B: each diagram node carries the number of the step it belongs to, it separates HTTP calls that wait for a reply from broker events, and it spells out who replies to whom and when, so I can follow the whole request without guessing; A is tidier but leaves those mechanics vague and sends refund outcomes through the charge webhook decision in a way that is harder to trace.

author: sonnet
reason: A covers more of the system, including timeouts, crash recovery, out-of-order payments and strict hold expiry, in consistent tables that are easy to scan, and its flow agrees with itself. B is friendlier at first glance, with a diagram legend and a per-service storage table, but it mixes an HTTP reserve with an event reply and adds a conditional re-take of unsold stock that makes the model harder to follow.

author: sonnet
reason: B says outright that Order coordinates, explains how the outbox relay works, and has a failure table covering timeouts, crashes, out-of-order payment success and refund retries, so a newcomer gets a fuller and more checkable picture of the system than from A's cleaner but thinner happy-path-plus-branches account.
